stages.title: Oceans, seas and marine environments
stages.hook: If you looked at Earth from space, what colour would most of it be? Why do you think so?
explain: Most of our planet is covered by salty water. The biggest areas of water are called oceans. There are five: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic.
Seas are smaller parts of the ocean, often near land. The water in them is salty too. Salt is the reason sea water tastes bad and we cannot drink it.

Many plants and animals live in the sea: fish, crabs, whales and tiny floating plants. A place where living things make their home is called an environment. Reefs, beaches and the deep sea are all marine environments.

example.q: A fish is in a salty sea. Is it in an ocean, a pond or a river?
steps: Ponds and rivers are not salty.
Salty water in a very big place is the sea or ocean.

analogies.home: The ocean is like one huge bath that every beach on Earth is connected to.
analogies.nature: A coral reef is like a busy forest under the water, full of homes for animals.
analogies.sea: Boats can sail from one country to another because the oceans join together.
analogies.city: A harbour is like a big front door where the sea meets the town.

stages.mnemonic: Five oceans, five fingers on a hand: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic.
terms: A very big area of salty water.
A smaller part of the ocean, often next to land.
The white stuff that makes sea water taste strong.

misc.wrong: The sea is just a very big lake.
misc.right: A lake is usually fresh water on land. The sea is salty and joins up with the whole world ocean.

stages.limits: People count the oceans in different ways. Some say four, some say five, and some say there is one world ocean.

trip.prompt: Look at the map of the oceans. Find the biggest one.

questions.q: Which is the biggest ocean?
questions.why: The Pacific Ocean is the biggest of all.

questions.q: How does sea water taste?
questions.why: Sea water has salt in it, so it tastes salty.

questions.q: Why should we not drink sea water?
o: It is too cold and makes our teeth hurt
It has too much salt for our bodies
It has no water in it, only sand and salt
questions.why: Too much salt is bad for our bodies. We drink fresh water instead.

questions.q: What covers most of the Earth?
questions.why: Ocean water covers most of our planet.

questions.q: Which one is a marine place?
questions.why: A coral reef is in the sea, so it is a marine place.

questions.q: Match each ocean to a clue.
questions.why: The Pacific is the biggest. The Arctic is icy and in the far north. The Southern Ocean circles Antarctica.

questions.q: Put these from smallest to biggest.
questions.why: A puddle is tiny, a pond is bigger, a sea is huge and the ocean is the biggest.

questions.q: Rain falls on a hill and runs into a stream, then a river. Where does the river water often end up?
questions.why: Rivers flow downhill and many of them end in the sea.

questions.q: A girl wants to sail from one continent to another. What must her boat cross?
questions.why: Continents are separated by oceans, so she must cross one.

questions.q: A crab lives on a beach. Why does it need the sea nearby?
o: The sea is its home and food place
It cannot walk on sand without the sea
It likes to drink milk from the sea
It wants to be a fish one day
questions.why: Animals live where they find food and shelter. The sea gives the crab both.

panel.q: Why is the sea salty but the rain is not?
o: Rivers carry tiny bits of salt to the sea and the water leaves as vapour but salt stays
Someone adds salt to the sea
Rain washes the salt out of the sky
panel.why: Water that evaporates leaves salt behind, so over a very long time the sea became salty.

panel.q: A lake has no salt. Is it a sea?
o: No, a sea is salty and joined to the ocean
Yes, all water that is wide is a sea, even in a lake
Yes, if it is big and has waves on it, it is a sea
No, because lakes have no fish
panel.why: Seas are salty and part of the ocean. A fresh lake is different.

panel.q: Why is it important to keep the sea clean?
o: Many animals and people need it
Sea water is never used by anyone
panel.why: Sea animals live there and people get food and travel from the sea.

teach.model: The ocean is a very big area of salty water that covers most of the Earth. It has five main parts, like the Pacific and the Atlantic. Fish, crabs and whales live in it. We must keep it clean.

points.ask: What is special about the water?

stages.title: Floating and sinking
stages.hook: A heavy ship floats, but a tiny pebble sinks. How can that be?
explain: Some things float on water and some things sink. A wooden stick floats. A coin sinks.
Water pushes up on things. This push is called buoyancy. If the push is big enough, the thing floats.
Shape matters too. A flat lump of clay sinks, but if you make it into a boat shape with a hollow, it can float. The hollow holds air, and air is light.

example.q: A ball of clay sinks. How can you make it float?
steps: Clay is heavy for its size.
Make it into a bowl shape with air inside.
Now it pushes aside more water, so water pushes up more.

analogies.home: In the bath, a plastic duck floats but a spoon sinks.
analogies.sport: A beach ball stays on top of the pool water, but it is hard to push down.
analogies.sea: A big ship floats because it is mostly hollow and full of air.
analogies.nature: A leaf floats on a pond because it is light and wide.

stages.mnemonic: Water pushes UP. Light and wide: float with pride. Heavy and small: sink and fall.
terms: To stay on top of the water.
To go down to the bottom.

misc.wrong: Big things always sink and small things always float.
misc.right: Size alone does not decide it. A huge ship floats and a tiny pebble sinks. It depends on shape and how heavy the thing is for its size.

stages.limits: In this world we keep the idea simple. Later you will learn the exact rule.

trip.prompt: Look at the pictures. Find something that floats and something that sinks.

questions.q: What do we call the push of water upward?
o: The wind that blows across the water
The way a heavy thing goes down
The dark shape a boat makes on water
questions.why: Buoyancy is the upward push from water.

questions.q: Which will most likely float?
o: A coin, because it is small and flat
A stone, because it is round and smooth
A key, because it is light and thin
questions.why: Wood is light for its size, so it floats.

questions.q: Which will most likely sink?
questions.why: A pebble is heavy for its size, so it sinks.

questions.q: Why can a big ship float?
o: It has lots of air inside and a good shape
It is made of wood only, so it must float on top
It is very small, so the water can hold it up
The sea is flat, so nothing in it can sink
questions.why: A ship is mostly hollow, so it is light for its size and floats.

questions.q: Match the thing to what it does in water.
questions.why: Cork and toy boats are light for their size. Stones and coins are heavy for their size.

questions.q: You squash clay into a flat ball and it sinks. You shape it like a bowl and it floats. What changed?
o: The clay got lighter in weight
questions.why: The weight stayed the same but the bowl shape pushes away more water, so the water pushes up more.

questions.q: Put these in order of what happens when you drop a stone in a pond.
questions.why: The stone falls in, moves down through the water and stops at the bottom.

questions.q: A child wants a toy that floats. What should it be made of?
o: Iron, because it is strong and shiny
Stone, because it is hard and smooth
Glass marbles, because they are round
questions.why: Light materials like foam float.

questions.q: A boat gets a hole and water comes in. Why does it sink?
o: The air inside is pushed out and it gets heavier
The sea gets angrier and pulls the boat down
The sail falls down and drags the boat under
Boats always sink in the morning light and cold
questions.why: Water replaces the air inside, so the boat gets heavy and sinks.

questions.q: Which makes you float more easily?
o: Wearing a backpack full of stones
questions.why: A lifejacket is full of light material that helps you float.

panel.q: A tiny steel needle can float if laid very gently, yet a big steel ship floats. What is the safest simple idea for the ship?
o: Its shape holds a lot of air so it is light for its size
Steel is lighter than water, so it floats
Ships are held up by the wind in the sails
The sea is thicker than land, like jelly
panel.why: A ship has a hollow shape, so on average it is light for its size.

panel.q: Why do children wear armbands in a pool?
o: They hold air, which helps them float
They make the water warm around a child
They make children heavier so they stay calm
They are for fashion only and look nice
panel.why: Air in the armbands gives extra lift.

panel.q: A full cargo boat sits lower in the water than an empty one. Why?
o: More weight means it sinks in a bit more
It is angry and wants to hide in the water
Water is heavier on the left side of the boat
Full boats are always a smaller size than empty ones
panel.why: A heavier boat pushes aside more water, so it sits lower.

teach.model: Water pushes up on things. If a thing is light for its size, like wood or a hollow boat, the push is enough and it floats. A heavy small thing like a stone sinks.

points.ask: What does the water do to the thing?

stages.title: Ships and boats
stages.hook: Why do ships look so different from each other? Some are tall, some are flat, and some are tiny.
explain: A boat is usually small. A ship is big. Both float and carry people or things across water.

Different jobs need different ships. A fishing boat catches fish. A ferry carries people and cars. A cargo ship carries boxes called containers. A tanker carries oil. A tugboat is small but strong and pulls big ships.
Every ship has a hull, which is the body that floats. The front is called the bow and the back is called the stern. A strong engine or a sail makes it move.

example.q: A town needs to move many boxes of fruit to another country. Which ship is best?

analogies.city: A ferry is like a bus on the water. A cargo ship is like a lorry.
analogies.farm: A tugboat is like a small, strong tractor that pulls something heavier than itself.
analogies.home: The hull is like the bowl of a soup bowl: hollow and holding things.
analogies.sea: A fishing boat is the sea's farm vehicle: it goes out to gather food.

stages.mnemonic: Bow at the front, stern at the back; the hull holds all the stuff in the stack.
terms: The body of a ship that floats.

misc.wrong: All ships are the same, only the size is different.
misc.right: Ships are built for different jobs, so their shapes and equipment are different.

stages.limits: People often use the words boat and ship in different ways. There is no one rule for all places.

trip.prompt: Find three different types of ships and say what job each does.

questions.q: What is the front of a ship called?
questions.why: The bow is the front. The stern is the back.

questions.q: What is the back of a ship called?
questions.why: The stern is the back of a ship.

questions.q: Which ship carries people and cars across a short stretch of water?
questions.why: A ferry carries people and cars on regular trips.

questions.q: Which ship carries oil?
questions.why: A tanker has big tanks for oil.

questions.q: Match each ship to its job.
questions.why: Each ship is built for one main job.

questions.q: A big ship cannot turn in a small harbour by itself. What helps it?
questions.why: Tugboats are small and strong. They push and pull the big ship.

questions.q: Put the parts in order from the front to the back of a ship.
questions.why: The bow is at the front and the stern is at the back. The deck and engine room are in between.

questions.q: A family lives on a small island with no bridge. How can they get to town?
questions.why: A ferry crosses water, so it is the best way.

questions.q: Why does a ship have a hull shaped like a bowl?
o: So it holds air and floats
So it looks funny from far away
So it can fly over the waves
So it can roll over like a ball
questions.why: The hollow hull holds air, which helps it float.

questions.q: Why do fishing boats go out early in the morning?
o: To catch fish and bring them home fresh
To make big waves for the beach
To visit the moon before it gets dark
To dry clothes in the cool morning wind
questions.why: Fishers catch fish and want to bring them back to sell or eat while fresh.

panel.q: Why is a tugboat small but strong?
o: It has a powerful engine for its size
It is full of cargo that pushes it along
It is made of foam so it is light
It has no hull so it is fast
panel.why: A tug needs a strong engine to pull ships much bigger than itself.

panel.q: Why do cargo ships use big boxes called containers?
o: They stack neatly and are easy to lift
They are fun to play in at the port
They float away on the sea by themselves
They keep the sea water cold and calm
panel.why: Same-size boxes stack well and can be moved fast by cranes.

panel.q: A boat has a sail. What moves it?
panel.why: Wind pushes on the sail and moves the boat.

teach.model: Ships are built for jobs. A fishing boat catches fish. A ferry carries people. A cargo ship carries boxes. A tugboat pulls big ships. All of them have a hull that floats.

points.ask: How does a ship stay up?

stages.title: Waves and currents
stages.hook: Why does the sea move up and down at the beach? Is something pushing it?
explain: Waves are moving bumps on the water. Wind blowing across the sea makes most waves. A strong wind makes big waves.
A current is water that flows along in one direction, like a river in the sea. Currents can carry boats, fish and floating things a long way.
Waves look as if the water is travelling, but the water mostly goes up and down. A floating duck bobs up and down as a wave passes. It does not travel to the shore with the wave.

example.q: The wind blows hard over the sea all day. What will the waves be like?

analogies.home: Blow gently on a cup of tea. Little ripples come. That is how wind makes waves.
analogies.sport: A crowd doing a wave in the stadium moves around, but each person only stands up and sits down.
analogies.nature: A leaf on a stream moves with the flow, like a boat in a current.
analogies.music: A wave is like a long note that rises and falls, again and again.

stages.mnemonic: Wind makes waves; currents are rivers in the sea.
terms: A moving bump on the water.
Water that flows in one direction.

misc.wrong: Waves carry the water all the way to the beach.
misc.right: Water mostly moves up and down in a wave. The wave shape travels, not the water.

stages.limits: Some waves, like tsunamis, are made by other things, not by wind.

trip.prompt: Watch the pictures. How do big waves differ from small ones?

questions.q: What makes most sea waves?
questions.why: Wind blowing over the water makes most waves.

questions.q: What is a current?
o: A sea animal with a long tail
A kind of boat with a big sail
A wave that breaks on the beach
questions.why: A current is moving water, like a river in the sea.

questions.q: Bigger wind makes...
questions.why: More wind means more push, so waves grow.

questions.q: A duck sits on the water as waves pass. What does it do?
questions.why: The water mostly moves up and down, so the duck bobs.

questions.q: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: A moving bump on the water
questions.why: These are the three main words for this lesson.

questions.q: A bottle is dropped into a strong current. What will happen?
o: It is carried along with the water
It stays still forever in one place
It sinks right away to the bottom
It goes back to the shop by itself
questions.why: A current carries floating things along.

questions.q: Put these in order from calm sea to stormy sea.
questions.why: More wind makes more waves, so the sea gets rougher.

questions.q: Why do sailors check the weather before a trip?
o: Strong wind makes big waves that can be dangerous
Rain is boring and wet to watch
They want to see the clouds up high
Fish only bite on sunny days
questions.why: Big waves can be unsafe for small boats.

questions.q: A swimmer is near the shore on a day with big waves. What is the safest choice?
o: Swim far out where it is calm
Swim alone so nobody is in the way
Dive off the rocks into the waves
questions.why: Lifeguards know about waves and currents and can help.

questions.q: Why can a boat drift even when its engine is off?
questions.why: Moving water carries the boat along.

panel.q: A cork bobs up and down in waves but does not travel far. What does that tell us?
o: Water in a wave mostly moves up and down
Corks are very heavy things that sink
Waves are not real water moving at all
The cork is stuck to the sand below
panel.why: The wave shape moves along, while the water mostly goes up and down.

panel.q: Why are waves bigger far out at sea in a storm than in a small pond?
o: Wind has more water and space to push
Ponds are warmer than the sea, so waves stay small
Ponds have no wind at all, ever, so they stay still
Fish make the waves with their tails in a storm
panel.why: More open water lets wind build bigger waves.

panel.q: A swimmer is caught in a current that pulls away from the beach. What is a good idea?
o: Stay calm, float, and wave for help
Fight the current to swim straight back
panel.why: Staying calm saves energy. Floating and calling for help is safest.

teach.model: Wind blows on the sea and makes waves, which are moving bumps. A current is water flowing in one direction, like a river in the sea. Stronger wind makes bigger waves.

points.ask: What happens if the wind is strong?

stages.title: Ports and harbours
stages.hook: When a ship comes home, where does it stop? What is waiting for it there?
explain: A harbour is a calm, safe place for boats. It is often sheltered by land or by a strong wall called a breakwater. The wall stops big waves.
A port is a harbour with machines and buildings to load and unload ships. Cranes lift heavy boxes. Quays are the edges where ships tie up.
Ports are very important. Food, clothes and toys often travel by ship, then by lorry or train to a shop near you.

example.q: A ship arrives with 100 boxes. What lifts the boxes onto the quay?
steps: A crane is a strong lifting machine.

analogies.city: A port is like a bus station for ships.
analogies.home: A harbour is like a garage that keeps boats safe from the weather.
analogies.farm: A breakwater is like a fence that keeps the animals safe from the wind.
analogies.tech: Cranes at a port are like giant robot arms.

stages.mnemonic: Harbour is a hug for boats; the breakwater is the arms.
terms: A harbour with machines to load ships.
The edge where ships tie up.
A wall that stops big waves.

misc.wrong: Ships can stop anywhere and unload.
misc.right: Ships need a port with a quay and cranes, and deep enough water so they do not touch the bottom.

stages.limits: Some places have no big port, so goods arrive in smaller boats or by other routes.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a container port. Spot the cranes and the quay.

questions.q: What is a harbour?
o: A safe, sheltered place for boats
A kind of fish with a big mouth
A type of wave that rolls in
A big wind that blows from the sea
questions.why: A harbour keeps boats safe from big waves.

questions.q: What does a crane do at a port?
o: Catches fish with a long net
questions.why: Cranes lift heavy boxes on and off ships.

questions.q: What is a breakwater for?
questions.why: It is a wall that keeps big waves out of the harbour.

questions.q: Where do ships tie up?
questions.why: A quay is the edge of the port where ships tie up.

questions.q: Match each part of a port to its job.
questions.why: Each part helps ships stay safe or work.

questions.q: Why is it good for a harbour to have calm water?
o: Boats can stay still and be loaded safely
Fish get lost in calm water
Birds cannot land on the sea
questions.why: Calm water keeps boats steady while people work.

questions.q: Put the steps in order when a ship arrives.
items: Ship ties up at the quay
questions.why: First the ship arrives, then it is tied up, unloaded and the goods move on.

questions.q: Toys are made far away and come to your town by ship. Where do they get off the ship?
questions.why: Ports are where goods leave and join ships.

questions.q: A storm is coming. Why do boats go into the harbour?
o: It is sheltered from big waves
To see friends and have a chat
To get paint for the boat
To sleep in the warm sun
questions.why: A harbour protects boats from storm waves.

questions.q: Why do ships need deep water near the quay?
o: So the bottom of the ship does not hit the ground
So fish can fly up to the quay
So the quay itself can float
Because ships like the cold water
questions.why: A ship sits low in the water, so shallow water could trap it.

panel.q: A town has a harbour but no cranes. What problem would it have?
o: It would be hard to move heavy cargo
Boats could not float in the water at all
Waves would stop coming in to the town
Fish would leave the sea and never come back
panel.why: Without cranes, big boxes are hard to lift on and off ships.

panel.q: Why do many big cities grow around ports?
o: Trade and jobs come with ships
Ships make the city warm all year
Cities need waves to stay clean
People love noise from the boats
panel.why: Ports bring goods and work, so people settle nearby.

panel.q: Why is it good to keep a port clean of oil and rubbish?
o: It protects sea animals and people
Oil is good food for the fish
Nobody lives near ports so it is fine
panel.why: Spills and rubbish harm animals and the water.

teach.model: A port is a safe place where ships stop. It has a quay to tie up and cranes to lift boxes. A wall called a breakwater keeps big waves out.

stages.title: Offshore platforms
stages.hook: Far out in the sea there are giant buildings standing in the water. Who lives there, and what do they do?
explain: An offshore platform is a big structure in the sea, far from land. People work on it to get oil and gas from deep under the sea floor. Others make power from wind.
Some platforms stand on long legs fixed to the sea floor. Others float and are held in place by strong ropes and chains called moorings.
Workers travel there by helicopter or boat and stay for some days. They wear helmets and lifejackets, because safety comes first.

example.q: A platform is far from land. How can workers get there quickly?
steps: It is too far to walk or drive.
A boat is slow but possible.

analogies.city: A platform is like a small town in the middle of the sea, with beds, food and work.
analogies.home: Legs on the sea floor are like the legs of a table.
analogies.sea: A floating platform is like a ship that is tied down so it stays in one place.
analogies.tech: Wind turbines at sea are like giant fans in reverse: wind turns them to make electricity.

stages.mnemonic: Legs in the sea, or ropes to keep it free.
terms: Out in the sea, away from the shore.
A big structure with a flat top built in the sea.
Ropes or chains that hold a floating thing in place.
Many wind turbines that make electricity.

misc.wrong: Platforms just float anywhere they like.
misc.right: Platforms are fixed to the sea floor or held by moorings so they stay in the right place.

stages.limits: Oil and gas are fuels that can harm the air when burned. Many countries are building more wind power.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a platform. Look for the legs, the deck and the helipad.

questions.q: What is an offshore platform?
o: A big structure in the sea
A school bus that goes in the sea
A kind of fish with a flat body
A toy to play with on the beach
questions.why: It is a large structure built out at sea.

questions.q: How do workers often get to a far platform?
o: By bicycle along the sea floor
questions.why: It is far from land, so they use helicopters and boats.

questions.q: What holds a floating platform in place?
o: Sand castles on the sea bed
questions.why: Moorings are strong lines tied to anchors on the sea floor.

questions.q: What do wind turbines at sea make?
o: Waves that go back to the beach
Fish for the workers to eat
Salt for the kitchen at home
questions.why: Wind turns the blades and the turbine makes electricity.

questions.q: Match the word to what it means.
pairs: Lines that hold it in place
questions.why: These are words for things found on platforms.

questions.q: Why do workers on a platform wear lifejackets and helmets?
questions.why: Falls and splashes are possible, so safety gear protects them.

questions.q: Put these in order from the sea floor up.
questions.why: The legs stand on the sea floor and hold the deck above the waves; the helicopter pad is on top.

questions.q: Why is the deck of a platform built high above the water?
o: So big waves do not reach it
To see the moon and stars at night
To be near the birds that fly by
To save paint on the lower walls
questions.why: A high deck keeps equipment and people safe from waves.

questions.q: Why do people build wind farms at sea?
o: The wind is often strong and steady
There are no fish at sea to scare away
Land is always full of sand and rocks
The sea is quiet and still all year
questions.why: Strong steady wind makes more electricity.

questions.q: There is a storm and a helicopter cannot fly. What should the platform have ready?
o: Food, safety plans and a way to call for help
questions.why: Safe places need supplies and plans in case people cannot leave.

panel.q: A floating platform is held by lines. What would happen without them?
panel.why: Wind and current would push it away from the right spot.

panel.q: Why is oil spilling into the sea very bad?
o: It harms animals and spoils beaches
It makes fish stronger and helps them grow big
It cleans the water so swimmers can enjoy it
It makes waves smaller for ever and ever
panel.why: Oil coats animals and shores and can poison life.

panel.q: Why do platforms have strong fences and rails?
o: To stop people falling into the sea
panel.why: Rails protect people from falls.

teach.model: An offshore platform is a big structure out at sea. Some have legs on the sea floor and some float and are held by ropes. People work there to get oil and gas or make wind power, and safety comes first.

points.ask: What do workers do to be safe?

stages.title: Underwater pipelines
stages.hook: How can oil, gas or water travel from the middle of the sea to a town on land?
explain: A pipeline is a long pipe. Underwater pipelines lie on the sea floor and carry oil, gas or water from one place to another.
The pipe is made of strong steel and covered with a coating that helps stop rust. Rust is what happens when iron meets water and air for a long time.
Workers lay pipes from special ships. Robots called ROVs go down to look at the pipe. They check for leaks and damage so the sea stays clean.

example.q: A pipe lies in salty water for years. What might slowly happen to bare steel?
steps: So we cover the pipe with a coating.
example.a: It could rust, so it gets a coating

analogies.home: A pipeline is like the water pipe in your house, but much longer and under the sea.
analogies.city: It is like a motorway, but for liquids and gas.
analogies.farm: It is like a long hose that moves water to the fields.
analogies.tech: An ROV is like a drone, but it swims.

stages.mnemonic: Pipe on the floor, coat keeps rust out; the robot swims round to look all about.
terms: A long pipe that carries liquid or gas.
A red-brown crust that forms on iron or steel.
A robot that swims under the sea and is steered from a ship.
When something escapes through a hole.

misc.right: Sea water can slowly damage pipes, so people inspect them often.

stages.limits: Even a good pipe can be hit by an anchor or a fishing net, so people mark routes on maps.

trip.prompt: Look at how a pipe is laid from a ship. What does the ship do?

questions.q: What does a pipeline do?
questions.why: A pipeline moves liquid or gas from one place to another.

questions.q: What is an ROV?
o: A robot that works under the sea
questions.why: ROVs are robots steered from a ship.

questions.q: Why is a pipe covered with a coating?
o: To make the pipe look pretty
To make the pipe much heavier
To make the pipe float up high
questions.why: The coating keeps salty water off the steel.

questions.q: What is rust?
o: A crust that forms on iron or steel
questions.why: Rust forms when iron meets water and air.

questions.q: Match each thing to its job.
questions.why: Each helps move or protect what is in the pipe.

questions.q: A fisher finds an oily patch on the sea. What should she do?
o: Tell the coast guard or port at once
questions.why: A spill could come from a leak. Experts need to know quickly.

questions.q: Put these in order for building a pipeline.
items: Lay the pipe from a ship
questions.why: We build and protect the pipe before laying it, then inspect it.

questions.q: Why do ships not drop anchors near pipelines?
o: An anchor could hit and damage the pipe
questions.why: Heavy anchors can crush or drag a pipe.

questions.q: Why are pipes checked with a robot rather than a diver in very deep water?
o: It is too deep and dangerous for people
questions.why: Deep water has huge pressure and is dangerous, so robots go instead.

questions.q: A pipe is old and has a thin patch. What is a good plan?
o: Check it and repair it before it leaks
questions.why: Fixing problems early prevents spills.

panel.q: Why is salty water worse for steel than fresh water?
o: Salt makes steel soft like jelly
panel.why: Salty water carries electricity more easily, which speeds up rusting.

panel.q: A leak is found in a pipeline. What is the first aim?
o: Stop the flow and protect the sea
panel.why: Stopping the leak quickly reduces harm.

panel.q: Why do we draw pipelines on sea maps?
o: So ships and fishers can avoid them
To make the map look busy
panel.why: Maps help avoid damage to the pipe and to the people.

teach.model: A pipeline is a long pipe on the sea floor that carries oil, gas or water. It is made of strong steel with a coating to stop rust. Robots check it so it does not leak.

points.ask: Why does it need a coating?

stages.title: Marine life and ocean protection
stages.hook: Turtles, whales and tiny plankton all share the sea. What could we do to keep them safe?
explain: The ocean is home to huge numbers of living things, from tiny plankton to the blue whale. Plankton make much of the oxygen we breathe and feed many animals.
People can harm the sea. Rubbish like plastic bags can hurt turtles and birds. Oil spills coat animals. Too much fishing can leave too few fish.
We can protect the ocean. We can put rubbish in bins, use less plastic, fish only what the sea can replace, and clean beaches. Engineers make ships and platforms that spill less and make less noise.

example.q: You find a plastic bag on the beach. What should you do?
steps: Pick it up safely and put it in a bin.

analogies.home: The ocean is our shared home, so we keep it tidy like our own room.
analogies.nature: A coral reef is a city of animals. Taking away one part hurts the others.
analogies.farm: Taking only a few fish at a time is like picking ripe fruit and leaving the tree.
analogies.city: Bins and recycling in a town keep the streets clean. The same helps the sea.

stages.mnemonic: Bin it, do not throw it. The sea is not a bin.
terms: Tiny living things that float in the sea.
Dirty or harmful things in the air, land or water.
Make something old into something new.
The natural home of a plant or animal.

misc.wrong: The ocean is so big that our rubbish does not matter.
misc.right: Rubbish adds up and travels far on currents. Everyone's small actions matter.

stages.limits: Scientists are still learning how much life lives in the deep sea.

trip.prompt: Find one animal that people are working to protect, and say what helps it.

questions.q: What is plankton?
o: Tiny living things floating in the sea
questions.why: Plankton are tiny plants and animals that drift in the sea.

questions.q: Which thing can hurt sea turtles?
questions.why: Turtles can mistake plastic for food and be hurt.

questions.q: What should you do with rubbish on the beach?
questions.why: Bins keep rubbish from reaching the sea.

questions.q: Where do many sea animals live?
o: In habitats like reefs and seaweed beds
questions.why: A habitat is the natural home of an animal.

questions.q: Match the harm to the animal it hurts.

questions.q: Why should we use less single-use plastic?
o: Fish learn to eat the plastic
More bags are made each week

questions.q: Put these in the order they happen to a plastic bottle that is thrown away carelessly.
items: Rain washes it into a drain

o: They grow up and make more fish
They taste bad to every other animal
They are shy and want to hide away
They are too colourful for the sea

questions.q: A beach has lots of rubbish after a storm. What can a class do?
o: Pick it up safely with adults and recycle

panel.q: A town is far from the sea. Can its rubbish still harm the ocean?
o: Yes, rivers and wind can carry it there
panel.why: Rubbish can travel through drains and rivers to the sea.

panel.q: Why do some countries make marine parks where fishing is not allowed?

To make the water look blue
To catch more fish for lunch

panel.q: Why does plankton matter to people?

teach.model: The ocean is home to many animals. Plastic and oil can hurt them. We protect the sea by putting rubbish in bins, using less plastic, and taking only a few fish.

points.ask: What can we do to help?

stages.title: Basic marine safety
stages.hook: You are going on a boat for a day. What should you do before the boat leaves the shore?
explain: The sea can be fun but it can also be dangerous. Water is deep, cold and moving. Staying safe starts before the trip.
Always wear a lifejacket on a boat and near deep water. Go with an adult. Check the weather. Tell someone on land where you are going and when you will be back.
If someone falls in the water, shout for help and throw something that floats, like a ring or a bottle. Do not jump in after them. Stay calm and call an adult or the coast guard.

example.q: A friend falls off a jetty into deep water. What do you do first?
steps: Do not jump in, because you could be in danger too.
Throw something that floats, like a ring.
example.a: Shout for help and throw something that floats

analogies.home: A lifejacket is like a seat belt for the water.
analogies.city: Safety rules on the sea are like traffic lights on a road.
analogies.sport: Players wear helmets and pads. People on boats wear lifejackets.
analogies.sea: A lighthouse warns sailors of rocks, like a big torch.

stages.mnemonic: Jacket on, tell someone, check the sky, throw, shout, do not go.
terms: A jacket that helps you float.
People who rescue others at sea.
A floating ring you can throw to someone.
A prediction of wind, rain and waves.

misc.wrong: Good swimmers do not need a lifejacket.
misc.right: Even strong swimmers can get tired or hurt in cold, rough water, so everyone should wear one on a boat.

stages.limits: Safety rules can differ between places, so always follow local advice and signs.

trip.prompt: Look at pictures of lifejackets and find the parts that help you float.

questions.q: What should you wear on a boat?
questions.why: A lifejacket helps you float if you fall in.

questions.q: Who should you go to the sea with?
questions.why: An adult can help you if something goes wrong.

questions.q: Someone falls in the water. What should you throw?
o: Something that floats, like a ring
questions.why: A floating ring helps them stay up until help comes.

questions.q: Why do we check the weather before a boat trip?
o: Storms can make the sea dangerous
questions.why: Strong wind and waves are risky for small boats.

questions.q: Match each safety item to its use.
questions.why: Each one helps keep people safe near the sea.

questions.q: Put these in the right order if a friend falls in deep water.
items: Wait for adults and the rescuers
questions.why: Call for help first, then give them something to hold. Keep your eyes on them. Do not jump in.

questions.q: Why should you tell someone on land where your boat is going?
o: They can get help if you do not come back
They will give you a prize for swimming
They can show you how to swim fast
They know where the best shells are
questions.why: If you are late, they know where to look.

questions.q: Why should you not jump in to save a friend?
o: You may get into danger too
The lifeguard will be cross with you
You may become very tired and hungry
The water gets warmer if you do

questions.q: The water is cold and a child is a good swimmer. Should they still wear a lifejacket on a boat?
o: Yes, cold water can make anyone tired fast
No, good swimmers never get tired
questions.why: Cold water saps strength quickly, so a lifejacket is important for everyone.

questions.q: You see a red flag at the beach. What does it often mean?

panel.q: Which is safer on a small boat?
o: Sitting down and holding on in waves
Standing up quickly and waving your arms
Swimming away from the boat as fast as you can
Jumping up and down in waves

panel.q: Why is a bright colour good for a lifejacket?

panel.q: A boat has a leak. What is a good first move?
o: Put on lifejackets and call for help
panel.why: Safety gear and a call for help come first.

teach.model: On a boat, wear a lifejacket and go with an adult. Check the weather and tell someone where you are going. If someone falls in, shout for help and throw something that floats. Do not jump in.
